plain: Hot gas is less dense than cool gas, so on Earth it rises. In a flame this rising flow drags air in and shapes the flame. In microgravity there is almost no buoyant rise, so other flows — ventilation, diffusion, electric fields — dominate.
A flame where fuel and oxidiser meet and burn where they mix, rather than being pre-mixed. A candle is the everyday example. Most of the investigations here study non-premixed (diffusion) flames.
source: Space Station's Quest for the Secrets of Fire, NASA

plain: Moving air changes how a flame spreads. In microgravity, fans or cabin airflow can be the main reason a flame continues to grow; stopping ventilation is an established spacecraft firefighting step.
The lowest oxygen concentration, in a given mixture and configuration, that will support steady burning. It is not a single universal number: pressure, diluent, material and flow all change it.

A weak, low-temperature flame (peak temperatures roughly 500–1000 K in the CFI-G description) that can burn fuel without the hot, bright combustion usually associated with fire. Cool flames matter for ignition and engine chemistry, and they can appear in droplet experiments.

Smoke is not one substance. Hydrocarbon fuels tend to make soot particles; plastics can make droplets of recondensed polymer fragments. Particle size affects whether a detector alarms — a key question for SAME and DAFT.
source: Combustion Science page, NASA Glenn (SAME summary)

plain: Gravity levels below Earth's. Microgravity is close to weightless; the Moon is about one-sixth of Earth's gravity and Mars about 0.38. Flames at reduced gravity can differ in shape, spread rate and extinction because buoyant flow is weaker or absent.
source: NASA NSSDC Moon and Mars fact sheets, and NASA combustion science overview
